To estimate how often the page has at least one slow call, we can use the concept of the "birthday problem" in probability theory, which is often used to estimate the probability of at least one event occurring out of a set of independent events.

Given that each call independently exceeds 10 ms one percent of the time, we can calculate the probability of a single call being slow as 0.01.

The probability of the page having at least one slow call can be estimated using the formula for the probability of at least one success in n independent trials, which is 1 minus the probability of no successes in n trials. This is given by:

P(at least one slow call) = 1 - (probability of no slow calls in all 10 trials)

Since each call is independent, the probability of no slow calls in a single trial is (1 - 0.01) = 0.99. Therefore, the probability of no slow calls in 10 trials is (0.99)^10.

P(at least one slow call) = 1 - (0.99)^10 ≈ 0.1044

This means that approximately 10.44% of the time, the page will have at least one slow call.

This has significant implications for tail latency targets. If the page is expected to handle a large volume of requests, even a small percentage of slow calls can result in a significant number of users experiencing poor performance. In this case, the 10.44% probability of at least one slow call translates to a 10.44% chance of users experiencing slow page loads, which can be unacceptable for many applications.

To mitigate this, the application can consider strategies such as:

* Increasing the number of backend instances to reduce the likelihood of slow calls
* Implementing caching or content delivery networks (CDNs) to reduce the load on backend servers
* Optimizing backend code to reduce the likelihood of slow calls
* Implementing retry mechanisms to handle slow calls
* Monitoring and alerting to detect slow calls and take corrective action
